summary: Defines the manifest for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI): a signed file listing all the signed objects at a publication point in an RPKI repository. This lets relying parties check that they have everything an authority has published. It obsoletes RFC 6486. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: An RPKI manifest is a signed list of the objects a certificate authority publishes. A relying party checks the list, dates and file hashes to find missing, replaced or changed files.

questions: how do relying parties detect missing rpki objects

what happens when an rpki fetch fails
how does a relying party check a manifest
subtitle: A signed inventory that helps relying parties detect missing or replaced RPKI files.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures detect changes to an object but do not show whether a valid older object replaced a newer one or an object was removed.
tldr.mechanism: A CA signs a manifest listing files at its publication point with a hash for each file. A relying party checks that the manifest is current and that all listed files can be retrieved and match their hashes.
tldr.outcome: A failed fetch requires a warning and use of cached data when available. RFC 9286 obsoletes RFC 6486 and the unit metadata says RFC 9981 updates it.

today: RFC 9286 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It obsoletes RFC 6486 and was updated by RFC 9981.

sections.title: Why RPKI Uses Manifests
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) stores signed objects in repositories. A signature can reveal that an object was altered, but it cannot by itself reveal that an unexpired older version was substituted or that an object was removed during retrieval.

A manifest is a signed object that lists the files at a certificate authority's publication point and gives each file's name and content hash. Relying parties use it to check repository contents, including when the retrieval channel is not secure. This RFC obsoletes RFC 6486.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can show that a file changed, but not that a newer file is missing. The manifest lists what the repository should contain so a relying party can check for missing or older files.

sections.title: Which Objects a Manifest Lists
sections.content:
A CA's manifest lists its published, non-expired and non-revoked certificates, its most recent Certificate Revocation List (CRL), and signed objects that can be verified with end-entity certificates issued by that CA. The manifest does not list itself because its hash cannot be calculated before it is signed.

The end-entity certificate used to verify a signed object is carried inside that object's Cryptographic Message Syntax wrapper, so it need not be published separately. If multiple CA instances share a publication point during key rollover, each manifest covers only the products of its own CA instance.
sections.plainLanguage: A manifest lists the current certificates, CRL and signed objects published by one CA instance. It excludes itself and does not combine the lists of separate CA instances that share a directory.

sections.title: Manifest Fields and File Names
sections.content:
The manifest content uses ASN.1 encoded with Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). Its fields are version, manifest number, creation time (thisUpdate), next scheduled update (nextUpdate), hash algorithm identifier and a list of file names with hashes. Version MUST be 0. The manifest number increases by 1 for each new manifest, and verifiers MUST handle values up to 20 octets.

Each file name has a name made from letters, digits, hyphens or underscores, then one dot and a three-letter extension listed in the RPKI repository name registry. Certificate authorities and relying parties MUST preserve case and treat names as case-sensitive. The manifest's content-type identifier is 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.26.
sections.plainLanguage: The manifest records its version and number, its dates, the hash method and a name-and-hash entry for each file. File names preserve letter case, and the version value is fixed at zero.

sections.title: Creating and Publishing a Manifest
sections.content:
A CA creates a new key pair and a one-time-use end-entity certificate for each manifest version. It MUST use a key pair to sign only one manifest and destroy the private key after signing. The certificate's validity interval matches the manifest's update interval, and the certificate for the replaced manifest is revoked.

The CA builds a file list from the objects at the publication point, signs and publishes the manifest there, and MUST publish a new manifest before nextUpdate and when published objects change. A repository operator MUST reduce the chance that a relying party sees an inconsistent intermediate state while files and manifest are being updated.
sections.plainLanguage: For every new manifest, the CA creates a new signing key, publishes the signed list, and destroys that key. It updates the list when files change and before the listed next-update time.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Validate a Fetch
sections.content:
A relying party obtains the manifest named in the CA certificate, checks that its content type and version are valid, and confirms that the current time falls between thisUpdate and nextUpdate. It also checks that the manifest number and creation time are newer than previously validated values.

The relying party retrieves every listed file from the same publication point and checks each file's hash. A missing file, invalid or stale manifest, or hash mismatch makes the fetch fail. The relying party MUST issue a warning and SHOULD notify an operator. It SHOULD continue using cached objects until they become stale or a later fetch succeeds, and MUST NOT validate subordinate objects in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: The relying party checks the manifest's dates and number, retrieves every listed file, and compares each hash. If any check fails, it warns and keeps usable cached data instead of validating new subordinate objects.

sections.title: Protection and Its Limits
sections.content:
Manifests help detect a removed, hidden or superseded repository object and help identify missing, extra or older files. They do not repair repository damage. A relying party learns about changes when it fetches the publication point.

The signed manifest and its update time help detect attempts to alter or hide a manifest within the normal update schedule. Replays within shorter time periods are not necessarily detectable from the manifest structure alone.
sections.plainLanguage: A manifest can reveal that repository contents do not match the signed list, but it cannot restore a missing file. Some replays within a manifest's validity period may not be detected.
